THOUGHT: The clinical picture is of a previously healthy 7-year-old with 3 weeks of fever and painful, necrotic papules that coalesce into widespread ulcers, refractory to antibiotics and systemic steroids. There was a recent streptococcal pharyngitis and influenza A (potential triggers). Inflammatory markers are elevated (CRP) and a marked cytokine elevation (IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IFN-γ, TNF-α) consistent with a pronounced systemic inflammatory response. Importantly, skin biopsy on three separate occasions was reported as consistent with PLEVA. Taken together, the history (febrile, ulceronecrotic eruption), exam (painful necrotic papules → ulcers), supportive histopathology, and cytokine profile point most strongly to the severe, systemic ulceronecrotic variant of PLEVA known as febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha–Habermann disease (FUMHD). 

Other entities can mimic this presentation (epidermal necrosis with systemic symptoms), so the top differentials include classic PLEVA (less fulminant form), severe mucocutaneous drug reactions (Stevens–Johnson syndrome/TEN spectrum), cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis with ulceration, and infectious necrotic dermatoses (eg, ecthyma gangrenosum or disseminated deep infections). Each is listed below in order of likelihood with brief rationale.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha–Habermann disease (FUMHD) — most likely: severe, ulceronecrotic variant of PLEVA presenting with fever, painful necrotic papules/ulcers, systemic inflammation and cytokine elevation; concordant skin biopsy on three occasions supports this diagnosis.
2. Pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA), classic (less severe) — closely related diagnosis; biopsy-consistent findings make PLEVA-spectrum disease very likely, with FUMHD representing the fulminant end.
3. Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) — can cause febrile, painful necrotic/erosive skin lesions and systemic inflammation; considered because of widespread necrosis, but histology and repeated PLEVA diagnoses make SJS/TEN less likely.
4. Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis (necrotizing leukocytoclastic vasculitis or vasculopathy) — can produce painful purpuric papules that ulcerate with systemic symptoms; would be considered if biopsy had shown vasculitic changes or if other organ systems were involved.
5. Infectious ulcerative dermatoses (eg, ecthyma gangrenosum from Pseudomonas or disseminated bacterial/fungal infection) — can produce necrotic ulcers and systemic illness; less likely given normal CBC/CMP, lack of response to antibiotics, and biopsy favoring PLEVA.
